en: Had been matched against the wrestler:
If he threw him, he would win the prize;
If he fell, he would be left with nothing.
Your elder's lament
The lion Manas heard.
As soon as the leopard heard it,
From atop his saddle,
From beneath his saddle cushion,
Bloodthirsty Manas, that noble lion,
Said, “Let my elder wear these when he grapples,”
The splendid, finely made kandagai
He took out there.
Manas's splendid wife Kanykei,
A strong maid almost like a saint,
Had lined its inside with brocade;
Sixty young wives gathered
And worked on it through the nights.
She had the whole earth searched,
And had mountain goats from the high mountains
Brought at her word.
Fitting it for the hero,
So the mighty man could wear it when wrestling,
She had made it in earnest.
Kanykei, wondrous in every way,
For fully six months
Had it steeped in tanning solution.
She finished all its seams
And wrapped them with silk.
So he could wear it when strength was needed,
She had intended it for your elder.
Young wives cut it and maidens sewed it;
The finest needlewomen sewed it.
The fairy-like Aruuke,
Who had tested five hundred young wives,
And capable kinswoman Kanykei
Had the defective parts unstitched;
They filed down steel
And poured it in, plate after plate.
It wearied the hand that held it;
A musket ball could not penetrate it,
But lodged in its midst.
It bent when grasped;
When its wearer thrashed in fury,
All the wrestlers
Lost their holds, one after another.
Embers could not pass through it when firewood burned;
The magnanimous one's kandagai
Could not be pierced when a cannon fired.
Its waistband was tied securely;
The auspicious kandagai
Had embroidered cuffs.
Its inside was brocade, patterned like lark's eyes.
There among the people,
Prince Manas the leopard
Was now about to give it to Koshoi.
Taking the kandagai in his hand,
Making his dun horse prance,
The noble hero
Now went up to Koshoi.
He turned Akkula's head.
Your elder, old Koshoi,
Your magnanimous blue-maned Manas,
Now stood voicing his sorrows.
“My elder, my old Koshoi,
The one among the Muslims whom I hold above all,
My saint who stands watching over me!
You brought down
The five pillars of fortified Beijing;
You laid low many
Of the Black Chinese who faced you.
His blessing enriched the people,
The old man who was like a prophet,
A saint born surpassing
All the sons of humankind.
My worthy child Kanykei knew
That you would grapple
With the infidel before the Muslims;
Saying, “My elder khan will wear it then,”
She had long kept it for you.
Its drawstring is secured with leather;
Its price is dear and its worth is great.
This forlorn kandagai
Is worth half the treasury's goods.
She tanned it and worked it supple,
Your sorrowing child Kanykei;
Saying, “At last he will give his blessing,”
She made it for you, elder.
If you accept the kandagai trousers
And give me your solemn blessing,
Here is why your blessing is needed:
I have many dark-ridged mountains,
And many foes with whom I fight.
I have many mountain passes where I gird myself,
And many places where I must face the enemy.
The Russians are on my right;
The Chinese are on my flank.
Guns confront me straight ahead;
I have many enemies with whom I contend.
Elder Koshoi, hear my words:
One who is here today is gone tomorrow;
Such filth is this world.
There is no way to resist
The Creator's command.
Though I have lived to this age,
I have no son behind me.
The horses on the ridge have mottled heads;
The swift argamaks have no master.
If my precious eyes close,
They have no owner to tend them.
Elder Koshoi, my old man,
My saintly kinsman who grants prayers,
Death may come on any of the seven days.
If I take up my spear and break the ranks,
If my allotted fate overtakes me
And death takes me in a bullet's flight,
Who will whet the black-bladed battle-ax
Without letting its edge grow dull?
If these people are left behind,
There is no son to be their protector;
Who will lead them without causing grief?
Who will whet the hawthorn-handled battle-ax
Without letting its edge turn?
If I pass from this world,
Who will lead these sorrowing people
And keep them from scattering?
Blue-maned elder Koshoi,
There is no way to resist
The Creator's command.
If my eyes close upon this world,
I have no son behind me as a protector.
When I reached the age of twelve,
When I did as I saw fit,
When I drove away all the Manchus and Chinese,
Root and branch,
When I unleashed the great slaughter
And ravaged their women and girls,
Taking them as booty,
Karabörk, daughter of Khan Kayyp,
Was the wife I chose and took.
How many years has she been with me?
It is plain what burden she has borne:
She droops and does not comb her hair;
Her heels have never bled.
Such a grievous day has come.
Is it good for a man
To keep taking clever women as wives?
Elder Koshoi, old man,
Hear my answer clearly.
When I slaughtered the Kyzylbash people,
Because the Kyzylbash people ran wild
And committed their outrages, I slaughtered them.
When I overran
The khan's citadel and treasury,
Plundered their abundant livestock,
And scattered it among the people,
Akylay, daughter of Khan Shooruk,
That rustling infidel woman,
Was the wife I seized.
I have had no child by her.
Yesterday, in the city of Bukhara,
Loading gold and jewels by the batman,
Saying, “If I pay a bride-price, she will bear a child,”
I became a bridegroom and scattered livestock.
The youngest of twelve daughters,
A servant beloved by God,
The beauty among dark-complexioned women,
The radiant one among Muslims,
Kanykei, daughter of Kara Khan,
Was the wife I chose and took,
Paying a bride-price and giving livestock.
I have had no child by her.
God creates every living soul.
Blessed elder, hear my words:
They used to say a man would not pass away without a son,
Yet I am passing away childless.
Elder Koshoi, I have a plea;
I have a sorrow I must tell.
If you accept the kandagai trousers
And give me a sure blessing,
For a hero weighed down with grief,
Is there any night like the Night of Power?
I go about in sorrow,
My saintly elder khan;
Will a day come when I see a child?”
Hero Koshoi knew
That Manas's place was in heaven.
Saying, “The Creator will give him a child,”
Your blessed elder Koshoi
Smiled beneath his mustache.
The kandagai bestowed with honor—
Koshoi the leopard put it on.
The finest among needlewomen,
The most capable among women,
The noble woman Kanykei
Had made the kandagai to fit;
Mighty Koshoi put it on.
When it reached his calves,
The kandagai would go no farther.
Your elder's buttocks, huge as a millstone,
Would not fit into the kandagai.
When he pulled it upward, it would not
Come over his backside.
However he pulled, it did not reach.
Your commanding elder Koshoi
Then grew angry:
“Let them stretch out the temple hair
Of the woman who made this,
Of an infidel woman such as this,
And place in her hands
A letter of divorce.
She did not make the seat wide enough;
She did not make the cuffs broad enough.
That woman who made it so tight,
That God-stricken woman,
An infidel woman such as this—
Let them slit her soles and rub in salt,
Slit the crown of her head and put worms in it,
Dress her in a coarse felt coat,
Mount her on a bay mare,
And drive her away without another word!
Manas the lion, in his foolishness,
Had gone about thinking,
“I took a wife from among the people,”
But that towering great bloodthirsty man
Had truly been living as a bachelor.
She turned abundance into want;
Could there be a wife like this?
Is a woman of this sort
Fit to be called a wife?”
Speaking so, your elder
Let loose many kinds of cutting words
And said them openly.
They struck the swaggering bloodthirsty man
Like lead bullets.
Sultan Manas flew into a rage,
Raging there among the people.
He moved to seize and slaughter Kanykei,
To put her to death.
His eyes blazed fiercely like fire;
His thirst for blood truly seized him.
God now struck the bloodthirsty man:
“Beginning with Kanykei,
I will slaughter the women.
Rather than go on calling
All who wear white kerchiefs my wives,
I will put them all to the sword.”
His eyes blazed in fury;
His thirst for blood truly seized him.
His teeth, huge as gates, showed;
Venom poured from his mouth.
His anger was terrible, his venom strong;
He set straight anyone who crossed him.
The forty companions of Khan Manas said,
“God has struck the bloodthirsty man;
His thirst for blood has seized him.
All the women will be slaughtered,
